source.text: וַיִּבְרַ֣ח דָּוִ֔ד מִנָּי֖וֹת בָּרָמָ֑ה וַיָּבֹ֞א וַיֹּ֣אמֶר׀לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוֹנָתָ֗ן מֶ֤ה עָשִׂ֨יתִי֙ מֶֽה־עֲוֺנִ֤י וּמֶֽה־חַטָּאתִי֙ לִפְנֵ֣י אָבִ֔יךָ כִּ֥י מְבַקֵּ֖שׁ אֶת־נַפְשִֽׁי׃

records.literal_gloss: And fled David from Naioth in Ramah, and came and said before Jonathan, What have I done? What [is] my iniquity, and what [is] my sin before your father, that [he is] seeking my life?

en.L: And David fled from Naioth in Ramah, and he came and said before Jonathan, "What have I done? What [is] my iniquity, and what [is] my sin before your father, that he [is] seeking my life?"
en.B: David escaped from Naioth in Ramah and went to Jonathan. "What have I done?" he asked. "What is my crime? What wrong have I done to your father, that he is trying to take my life?"
en.R: David ran away from Naioth in Ramah. He went to Jonathan and asked him, "What have I done? What crime am I guilty of? What wrong have I done to your father? Why is he trying to kill me?"

decisions.choice: fled from Naioth in Ramah: David leaves Samuel's refuge
decisions.reason: David had fled to Samuel at Naioth in Ramah, and Saul's messengers and then Saul himself, coming to seize him, were overcome by the Spirit and prophesied (19:18-24). David uses the delay to escape. Naioth may mean "dwellings" or "camps"; it seems to name a place in or near Ramah where Samuel's prophets lived.

decisions.choice: iniquity and sin: any wrongdoing that would deserve punishment
decisions.reason: David uses two common words for wrongdoing, guilt and sin, to say that he has done nothing at all against Saul. He asks the same three questions that Jonathan will put to Saul in verse 32.

decisions.choice: seeking my life: trying to kill me
decisions.reason: To "seek someone's life" is a set way of saying that someone is out to kill them (22:23; 23:15; Exodus 4:19).

decisions.choice: crime; wrong
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use everyday words for the two terms for wrongdoing; Literal keeps "iniquity" and "sin".

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר ל֣וֹ חָלִילָה֮ לֹ֣א תָמוּת֒ הִנֵּ֡ה לֹֽא־יַעֲשֶׂ֨ה אָבִ֜י דָּבָ֣ר גָּד֗וֹל א֚וֹ דָּבָ֣ר קָטֹ֔ן וְלֹ֥א יִגְלֶ֖ה אֶת־אָזְנִ֑י וּמַדּוּעַ֩ יַסְתִּ֨יר אָבִ֥י מִמֶּ֛נִּי אֶת־הַדָּבָ֥ר הַזֶּ֖ה אֵ֥ין זֹֽאת׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said to him, Far be it! Not you will die. Look, not does my father a thing great or a thing small and not he uncovers my ear. And why would hide my father from me this thing? Not [is] this.

en.L: And he said to him, "Far from it! You will not die. Look, my father does not do anything great or anything small without uncovering my ear. And why would my father hide this thing from me? It [is] not so."
en.B: Jonathan answered, "Never! You are not going to die. My father does nothing, great or small, without telling me. Why would he hide this from me? It is not so."
en.R: "No!" Jonathan said. "You will not die! My father does not do anything, big or small, without telling me first. Why would he keep this a secret from me? It cannot be true."

decisions.choice: far be it: a strong denial
decisions.reason: The word means something like "unthinkable!" and is used to push away an idea as wrong or impossible (verse 9; 14:45; Genesis 18:25).

decisions.choice: uncover my ear: tell me, let me know
decisions.reason: Uncovering someone's ear was a picture for telling them something in confidence (9:15; 20:12-13; 22:8). Jonathan says his father keeps nothing from him.

decisions.choice: does not do: the reading noted in the margin
decisions.reason: At this point the consonants written in the Hebrew text and the reading the scribes noted in the margin differ slightly in the form of the verb ("has done" or "does"). The text follows the margin. Either way, Jonathan says that his father tells him everything he plans.

decisions.choice: it is not so: Jonathan rejects David's fear
decisions.reason: The two short words at the end mean "This is not [the case]." Jonathan sincerely believes his father has given up the plan, as Saul had sworn (19:6).

decisions.choice: telling me
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the picture "uncovering my ear"; Literal keeps the picture.

source.text: וַיִּשָּׁבַ֨ע ע֜וֹד דָּוִ֗ד וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ יָדֹ֨עַ יָדַ֜ע אָבִ֗יךָ כִּֽי־מָצָ֤אתִי חֵן֙ בְּעֵינֶ֔יךָ וַיֹּ֛אמֶר אַל־יֵֽדַע־זֹ֥את יְהוֹנָתָ֖ן פֶּן־יֵֽעָצֵ֑ב וְאוּלָ֗ם חַי־יְהוָה֙ וְחֵ֣י נַפְשֶׁ֔ךָ כִּ֣י כְפֶ֔שַׂע בֵּינִ֖י וּבֵ֥ין הַמָּֽוֶת׃

records.literal_gloss: And swore again David and said, Surely knows your father that I have found favor in your eyes, and he has said, Let not know this Jonathan, lest he be grieved. But truly, [as] lives Yahweh and [as] lives your soul, but like a step [is] between me and death.

en.L: But David swore again and said, "Your father knows well that I have found favor in your eyes, and he has said, 'Do not let Jonathan know this, or he will be grieved.' But truly, [as] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives and [as] your soul lives, [there is] but about a step between me and death."
en.B: But David answered him with an oath: "Your father knows very well that you think well of me, and he has said to himself, 'Jonathan must not know this, or it will grieve him.' But as surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives and as surely as you live, there is only a step between me and death."
en.R: But David made a solemn promise. He said, "Your father knows very well that you are my friend. So he has said to himself, 'Jonathan must not find out about this. It would upset him.' But I tell you, as surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives and as surely as you live, I am only one step away from death."

decisions.choice: swore again: answered with an oath
decisions.reason: David meets Jonathan's denial with an oath of his own. "Again" may mean that he swore a second time, or simply that he replied, now under oath, to what Jonathan had said.

decisions.choice: found favor in your eyes: you think well of me
decisions.reason: The phrase means that someone looks on another with kindness and goodwill (verse 29; 16:22). Saul knows how close his son is to David (18:1-4; 19:1-7).

decisions.choice: as Yahweh lives and as your soul lives: a double oath
decisions.reason: Swearing by the life of Yahweh is the strongest oath (14:39, 45; 19:6). David adds Jonathan's own life to it. "Your soul" here means simply "you" in person.

decisions.choice: about a step between me and death: I am close to being killed
decisions.reason: The picture is of a man who could fall into death with one step. Saul's spear had already missed David twice (18:11; 19:10).

decisions.choice: he has said to himself
decisions.reason: The verb "say" often means "think" or "say to oneself" (verse 26). David is guessing at Saul's reasoning, not reporting a speech.

source.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר יְהוֹנָתָ֖ן אֶל־דָּוִ֑ד מַה־תֹּאמַ֥ר נַפְשְׁךָ֖ וְאֶֽעֱשֶׂה־לָּֽךְ׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And said Jonathan to David, Whatever says your soul, and I will do for you.

en.L: And Jonathan said to David, "Whatever your soul says, I will do for you."
en.B: Jonathan said to David, "Whatever you want, I will do for you."
en.R: Jonathan told David, "I will do anything you want me to do."

decisions.choice: whatever your soul says: whatever you wish
decisions.reason: "Soul" here is the person's own desire (Deuteronomy 14:26). Jonathan places himself at David's disposal, as his covenant friend (18:3).

decisions.choice: whatever you want
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the idiom; Literal keeps "your soul says".

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר דָּוִ֜ד אֶל־יְהוֹנָתָ֗ן הִֽנֵּה־חֹ֨דֶשׁ֙ מָחָ֔ר וְאָנֹכִ֛י יָשֹׁב־אֵשֵׁ֥ב עִם־הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ לֶאֱכ֑וֹל וְשִׁלַּחְתַּ֨נִי֙ וְנִסְתַּרְתִּ֣י בַשָּׂדֶ֔ה עַ֖ד הָעֶ֥רֶב הַשְּׁלִשִֽׁית׃

records.literal_gloss: And said David to Jonathan, Look, [the] new moon [is] tomorrow, and I surely should sit with the king to eat; and you will send me away, and I will hide in the field until the evening, the third.

en.L: And David said to Jonathan, "Look, tomorrow [is the] new moon, and I ought to sit with the king to eat. But let me go, and I will hide myself in the field until the third evening.
en.B: David said to Jonathan, "Listen, tomorrow is the new moon festival, and I am expected to sit at the table with the king. But let me go, and I will hide in the field until the evening of the third day.
en.R: David said to Jonathan, "Look, tomorrow is the new moon festival. I am supposed to eat with the king. But let me go and hide in the field until the evening of the day after tomorrow.

decisions.choice: new moon: the feast at the start of the month
decisions.reason: The day of the new moon began each month. It was kept with offerings, trumpet blasts and a meal (Numbers 10:10; 28:11-15; 2 Kings 4:23). Here the king's household eats together for two days (verse 27), and David, as one of the king's own men, is expected to be there.

decisions.choice: I surely should sit: I am expected to sit
decisions.reason: The doubled verb stresses the obligation. David's absence will be noticed.

decisions.choice: until the third evening: until the evening of the day after tomorrow
alternatives: until the evening of the third day from tomorrow
decisions.reason: Counting today as the first day, the third day is the second day of the feast (verses 12, 19, 27, 34). David plans to stay hidden until Jonathan can bring word after both days.

decisions.choice: new moon festival
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "festival" so that the reader knows that the new moon was a feast day with a meal.

source.text: אִם־פָּקֹ֥ד יִפְקְדֵ֖נִי אָבִ֑יךָ וְאָמַרְתָּ֗ נִשְׁאֹל֩ נִשְׁאַ֨ל מִמֶּ֤נִּי דָוִד֙ לָרוּץ֙ בֵּֽית־לֶ֣חֶם עִיר֔וֹ כִּ֣י זֶ֧בַח הַיָּמִ֛ים שָׁ֖ם לְכָל־הַמִּשְׁפָּחָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: If surely misses me your father, and you will say, Asked urgently from me David to run [to] Bethlehem his city, for [the] sacrifice of the days [is] there for all the clan.

en.L: If your father misses me at all, then you will say, 'David earnestly asked leave of me to run [to] Bethlehem, his city, for the yearly sacrifice [is] there for the whole clan.'
en.B: If your father notices that I am missing, tell him, 'David begged me to let him hurry to Bethlehem, his hometown, because the whole clan is holding its yearly sacrifice there.'
en.R: If your father sees that I am not there, tell him, 'David asked me if he could hurry home to Bethlehem. His whole family is offering the yearly sacrifice there.'

decisions.choice: misses me: notices that I am absent
decisions.reason: The verb means to look for someone and find them missing. The same verb is used of David's empty seat in verses 18, 25 and 27.

decisions.choice: asked urgently: begged
decisions.reason: The doubled verb makes David's request sound pressing. Jonathan repeats it in verse 28.

decisions.choice: the sacrifice of the days: the yearly family sacrifice
decisions.reason: "The days" here means a yearly cycle, as with Elkanah's yearly sacrifice (1:21; 2:19). Bethlehem was the town of David's family (16:1-5; 17:12).

decisions.choice: family
decisions.reason: Readable uses "family" for the clan, the group of related households.

source.text: אִם־כֹּ֥ה יֹאמַ֛ר ט֖וֹב שָׁל֣וֹם לְעַבְדֶּ֑ךָ וְאִם־חָרֹ֤ה יֶֽחֱרֶה֙ ל֔וֹ דַּ֕ע כִּֽי־כָלְתָ֥ה הָרָעָ֖ה מֵעִמּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: If thus he says, Good, peace [is] to your servant; and if surely it burns to him, know that has been completed the evil from with him.

en.L: If he says thus, 'Good,' [there is] peace for your servant. But if he becomes very angry, know that harm has been determined by him.
en.B: Should he say, 'Good,' your servant is safe. But should he flare up in anger, you will know that he has made up his mind to do me harm.
en.R: If he says, 'All right,' then I am safe. But if he gets very angry, you can be sure that he has decided to hurt me.

decisions.choice: it surely burns to him: he flares up in anger
decisions.reason: Anger is spoken of as heat that burns (verse 30; 11:6). The doubled verb makes it strong.

decisions.choice: the evil has been completed: he has settled on harming me
decisions.reason: The verb means "to be finished" or "to be settled". The harm is decided and certain (verses 9 and 33; 25:17).

decisions.choice: your servant: a polite way of saying "me"
decisions.reason: Speaking of oneself as "your servant" was a common courtesy (Genesis 18:3). David uses it with the king's son, even though they are bound as friends.

decisions.choice: I; me
decisions.reason: Readable says "I" for the polite "your servant", which reads oddly in modern English.

source.text: וְעָשִׂ֤יתָ חֶ֨סֶד֙ עַל־עַבְדֶּ֔ךָ כִּ֚י בִּבְרִ֣ית יְהוָ֔ה הֵבֵ֥אתָ אֶֽת־עַבְדְּךָ֖ עִמָּ֑ךְ וְאִם־יֶשׁ־בִּ֤י עָוֺן֙ הֲמִיתֵ֣נִי אַ֔תָּה וְעַד־אָבִ֖יךָ לָמָּה־זֶּ֥ה תְבִיאֵֽנִי׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And you will do chesed with your servant, for into [a] covenant of Yahweh you have brought your servant with you. And if there is in me iniquity, kill me you; and to your father why this you bring me?

en.L: So deal [in] steadfast love with your servant, for you have brought your servant into a covenant of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} with you. But if there is iniquity in me, put me to death yourself. Why then should you bring me to your father?"
en.B: So show faithful love to your servant, because you brought your servant into a covenant with you before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. But if I am guilty, kill me yourself. Why hand me over to your father?"
en.R: So show me faithful love, because you made a covenant with me before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. But if I have done anything wrong, then kill me yourself! Why take me to your father?"

decisions.choice: chesed: loyal love that keeps faith with a bond
decisions.reason: Chesed is kindness that is owed and freely given within a relationship, here the covenant Jonathan made with David (18:3). It is the same word used of God's own love (Exodus 34:6) and of Ruth's loyalty (Ruth 1:8). David asks Jonathan to act on it.

decisions.choice: a covenant of Yahweh: the covenant of 18:3
decisions.reason: Jonathan had made a covenant with David because he loved him (18:3). It was made before Yahweh, who stands as its witness and guards it (verses 23, 42). David now calls it a covenant into which Jonathan himself "brought" him.

decisions.choice: kill me yourself: an emphatic "you"
decisions.reason: David adds the pronoun "you" for stress: if he is guilty, he would rather die at his friend's hand than be handed over to Saul.

decisions.choice: steadfast love (Literal); faithful love (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The word is rendered the same way throughout, as in Exodus 34:6 and Ruth 1:8.

decisions.choice: Why hand me over to your father?
decisions.reason: "Why bring me to your father?" means "why let your father be the one to deal with me?"

source.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר יְהוֹנָתָ֖ן חָלִ֣ילָה לָּ֑ךְ כִּ֣י׀אִם־יָדֹ֣עַ אֵדַ֗ע כִּֽי־כָלְתָ֨ה הָרָעָ֜ה מֵעִ֤ם אָבִי֙ לָב֣וֹא עָלֶ֔יךָ וְלֹ֥א אֹתָ֖הּ אַגִּ֥יד לָֽךְ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And said Jonathan, Far be it from you! For if surely I knew that had been completed the evil from with my father to come upon you, then not it would I tell you?

en.L: And Jonathan said, "Far be it from you! For if I knew for certain that harm had been determined by my father to come upon you, would I not tell you?"
en.B: Jonathan said, "Never think it! If I knew for certain that my father had decided to bring harm on you, would I not tell you?"
en.R: "Do not even think that!" Jonathan said. "If I found out that my father had decided to hurt you, of course I would tell you!"

decisions.choice: far be it from you: do not think such a thing
decisions.reason: As in verse 2. Here it rejects the thought that Jonathan could ever kill David or hand him over.

decisions.choice: would I not tell you?: a question that expects "yes"
decisions.reason: The clause has no question word, but it reads most naturally as a question expecting the answer "Of course I would."

decisions.choice: of course I would tell you!
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question into the statement it implies.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר דָּוִד֙ אֶל־יְה֣וֹנָתָ֔ן מִ֖י יַגִּ֣יד לִ֑י א֛וֹ מַה־יַּעַנְךָ֥ אָבִ֖יךָ קָשָֽׁה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And said David to Jonathan, Who will tell me, or what [if] answers you your father harshly?

en.L: And David said to Jonathan, "Who will tell me, or what if your father answers you harshly?"
en.B: David asked Jonathan, "Who will let me know if your father gives you a harsh answer?"
en.R: David asked Jonathan, "If your father answers you angrily, how will I find out?"

decisions.choice: who will tell me, or what: who will tell me if
decisions.reason: The two questions belong together: David cannot come near Saul's table, so he asks how word will reach him if Saul answers harshly. Jonathan answers this in verses 12-23.

decisions.choice: who will let me know if
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable join the two questions into one, which says the same thing more plainly.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהֽוֹנָתָן֙ אֶל־דָּוִ֔ד לְכָ֖ה וְנֵצֵ֣א הַשָּׂדֶ֑ה וַיֵּצְא֥וּ שְׁנֵיהֶ֖ם הַשָּׂדֶֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And said Jonathan to David, Come, and let us go out [to] the field. And went out the two of them [to] the field.

en.L: And Jonathan said to David, "Come, and let us go out [to] the field." And the two of them went out [to] the field.
en.B: Jonathan said to David, "Come, let us go out into the field." So the two of them went out together.
en.R: Jonathan said to David, "Come on, let us go out into the field." So they both went out there.

decisions.choice: the field: the open country outside the town
decisions.reason: "The field" is the land outside the town walls, used for crops and pasture. There the two could talk without being overheard, and Jonathan could show David the place for the signal (verses 19-22).

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוֹנָתָ֜ן אֶל־דָּוִ֗ד יְהוָ֞ה אֱלֹהֵ֤י יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ כִּֽי־אֶחְקֹ֣ר אֶת־אָבִ֗י כָּעֵ֤ת׀מָחָר֙ הַשְּׁלִשִׁ֔ית וְהִנֵּה־ט֖וֹב אֶל־דָּוִ֑ד וְלֹֽא־אָז֙ אֶשְׁלַ֣ח אֵלֶ֔יךָ וְגָלִ֖יתִי אֶת־אָזְנֶֽךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Jonathan to David, Yahweh, God of Israel! When I sound out my father about [this] time tomorrow, the third [day], and look, [it is] good toward David, then not will I send to you and uncover your ear?

en.L: And Jonathan said to David, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}}, [the] God of Israel, [be witness]! When I sound out my father about this time tomorrow, [or] the third [day], and look, [he is] good toward David, will I not then send to you and uncover your ear?
en.B: Then Jonathan said to David, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, is my witness! By this time tomorrow, or the day after, I will sound out my father. If he is well disposed toward David, I will certainly send word and let you know.
en.R: Jonathan said to David, "I promise this before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel. By this time tomorrow or the next day, I will find out what my father is thinking. If he feels good about you, I will send someone to tell you.

decisions.choice: Yahweh, God of Israel!: the opening of an oath
alternatives: Yahweh, God of Israel, is witness
decisions.reason: Jonathan begins by naming Yahweh, but the sentence does not say what Yahweh is to be. The sense is an appeal to Yahweh as witness to the promise that follows (compare verses 23 and 42). Some ancient translations add the word "witness".

decisions.choice: this time tomorrow, the third day: by tomorrow or the day after
decisions.reason: Jonathan will test Saul's mood over the two days of the feast: tomorrow, and the third day counting from today (verses 5, 19, 27).

decisions.choice: uncover your ear: tell you
decisions.reason: As in verse 2.

decisions.choice: good toward David: well disposed to him
decisions.reason: "Good" here means that Saul is favorable, with no harm in mind (compare verse 7).

decisions.choice: is my witness; I promise this before
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply the words that make the oath clear in English. Literal brackets them.

source.text: כֹּֽה־יַעֲשֶׂה֩ יְהוָ֨ה לִֽיהוֹנָתָ֜ן וְכֹ֣ה יֹסִ֗יף כִּֽי־יֵיטִ֨ב אֶל־אָבִ֤י אֶת־הָֽרָעָה֙ עָלֶ֔יךָ וְגָלִ֨יתִי֙ אֶת־אָזְנֶ֔ךָ וְשִׁלַּחְתִּ֖יךָ וְהָלַכְתָּ֣ לְשָׁל֑וֹם וִיהִ֤י יְהוָה֙ עִמָּ֔ךְ כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר הָיָ֖ה עִם־אָבִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Thus may do Yahweh to Jonathan and thus may he add, if it pleases my father [to bring] the evil upon you, and I will uncover your ear and send you away, and you will go in peace. And may be Yahweh with you as he was with my father.

en.L: Thus may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} do to Jonathan, and thus may {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} add, if my father is pleased [to bring] harm on you and I [do not] uncover your ear and send you away, so that you go in peace. And may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} be with you as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was with my father.
en.B: But if my father means to do you harm, may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} deal with me, Jonathan, ever so severely if I do not let you know and send you away to go in safety. May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} be with you as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has been with my father.
en.R: But if my father wants to hurt you, I will tell you and send you away safely. If I do not, may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} punish me terribly. And may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} be with you, as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was with my father.

decisions.choice: so may Yahweh do to Jonathan, and so may he add: a curse on oneself
decisions.reason: This is the form of a solemn oath: the speaker calls down punishment on himself if he fails to keep his word (3:17; 14:44; Ruth 1:17). The punishment is left unnamed. Jonathan speaks of himself by name.

decisions.choice: if my father intends harm and I do not tell you: what the oath binds Jonathan to
alternatives: if my father intends harm, I will tell you and send you away
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is compressed. Its sense is that Jonathan puts himself under the curse if, when he learns that Saul means harm, he fails to warn David and send him safely away. The word "not" is not written but is implied by the oath form.

decisions.choice: as he was with my father: Yahweh's presence that once marked Saul
decisions.reason: Yahweh had been with Saul at the start of his reign (10:7), but his Spirit had left Saul and now Yahweh is with David (16:13-14; 18:12, 14, 28). Jonathan's wish quietly accepts that David is the one Yahweh has chosen.

decisions.choice: may the LORD deal with me, Jonathan
decisions.reason: Jonathan names himself in the third person; Balanced keeps the name but makes clear that he is the speaker.

decisions.choice: I will tell you ... If I do not, may the LORD punish me
decisions.reason: Readable puts the promise first and the curse after it, so that the oath is easy to follow.

source.text: וְלֹ֖א אִם־עוֹדֶ֣נִּי חָ֑י וְלֹֽא־תַעֲשֶׂ֧ה עִמָּדִ֛י חֶ֥סֶד יְהוָ֖ה וְלֹ֥א אָמֽוּת׃

records.literal_gloss: And not if still I [am] alive, and not you will do with me [the] chesed of Yahweh, and not I will die?

en.L: And if I [am] still alive, will you not show me the steadfast love of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, so that I do not die?
en.B: And if I am still alive then, will you not show me the faithful love of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, so that I do not die?
en.R: If I am still alive then, please show me the faithful love of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, so that I am not killed.

decisions.choice: the three "nots": a plea in the form of a question
alternatives: O that, while I am still alive, you would show me the chesed of Yahweh
If I am still alive, you will not show me ... and I will not die (statements)
decisions.reason: The verse repeats "not" three times, and its grammar is hard. It is read here as a question that expects "yes": "If I am alive, will you not show me ... so that I do not die?" The first word could also be read with different vowels as "O that", giving a wish: "O that, while I am still alive, you would show me ...". The plea is the same either way.

decisions.choice: the chesed of Yahweh: loyal love such as Yahweh shows
decisions.reason: Chesed is loyal love within a bond (verse 8). "Of Yahweh" may mean love like Yahweh's own, or love that was pledged before Yahweh and that he will hold the parties to. Both point to faithfulness beyond what is usual.

decisions.choice: so that I do not die: Jonathan foresees a change of king
decisions.reason: When a new family took the throne, the old king's family was often put to death (1 Kings 15:29; 16:11; 2 Kings 10:11). Jonathan asks David, the future king, to spare him and his family.

decisions.choice: steadfast love (Literal); faithful love (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 8.

decisions.choice: please show me
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question into the request it implies.

source.text: וְלֹֽא־תַכְרִ֧ת אֶֽת־חַסְדְּךָ֛ מֵעִ֥ם בֵּיתִ֖י עַד־עוֹלָ֑ם וְלֹ֗א בְּהַכְרִ֤ת יְהוָה֙ אֶת־אֹיְבֵ֣י דָוִ֔ד אִ֕ישׁ מֵעַ֖ל פְּנֵ֥י הָאֲדָמָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And not you will cut off your chesed from with my house forever, and not when cuts off Yahweh the enemies of David, each from upon [the] face of the ground.

en.L: And do not cut off your steadfast love from my house forever, not even when {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} cuts off the enemies of David, each one from the face of the ground."
en.B: And never cut off your faithful love from my family, not even when {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has cut off David's enemies, every one of them, from the face of the earth."
en.R: And never stop showing faithful love to my family, not even when {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has wiped out every one of your enemies from the earth."

decisions.choice: cut off ... cuts off: a play on one verb
decisions.reason: The same verb is used twice: David must not "cut off" his love from Jonathan's family when Yahweh "cuts off" David's enemies. The verb is also the one used for "making" a covenant (verse 16; 18:3). Jonathan asks that David's victory, which he expects, should not sweep away his own family.

decisions.choice: my house: my family and descendants
decisions.reason: "House" means the household and the line that comes after it.

decisions.choice: forever: kept after Jonathan's death
decisions.reason: David remembered this oath when he was king. He sought out Jonathan's son Mephibosheth to show him chesed for Jonathan's sake (2 Samuel 9:1, 7) and spared him later (2 Samuel 21:7).

decisions.choice: steadfast love (Literal); faithful love (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 8.

decisions.choice: your enemies
decisions.reason: Jonathan speaks of "David's enemies" while speaking to David. Readable says "your enemies" so the reader does not wonder who is meant.

source.text: וַיִּכְרֹ֥ת יְהוֹנָתָ֖ן עִם־בֵּ֣ית דָּוִ֑ד וּבִקֵּ֣שׁ יְהוָ֔ה מִיַּ֖ד אֹיְבֵ֥י דָוִֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: And cut Jonathan with [the] house of David, and may require Yahweh from [the] hand of [the] enemies of David.

en.L: So Jonathan cut [a covenant] with the house of David, [saying], "May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} require [it] from the hand of David's enemies."
en.B: So Jonathan made a covenant with David's house, and said, "May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} call David's enemies to account."
en.R: So Jonathan made a covenant with David's family. He said, "May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} punish David's enemies."

decisions.choice: cut: made a covenant
decisions.reason: "Cut" is short for "cut a covenant", the usual way of saying "make a covenant" (11:1-2; 18:3; 22:8). The word "covenant" is left out, as it sometimes is.

decisions.choice: require from the hand of: call to account, punish
decisions.reason: To "require" something from someone's hand is to hold them responsible for it (Genesis 9:5; Ezekiel 3:18). The covenant now binds the two families, Jonathan's and David's.

decisions.choice: the words of the oath: Jonathan's curse, perhaps softened
alternatives: and Yahweh required it at the hand of David's enemies (narration)
may Yahweh call David to account (if he breaks it)
decisions.reason: The verb can be read as a wish spoken by Jonathan, as here, or as the narrator's statement that Yahweh did call David's enemies to account. In curses, scribes sometimes wrote "David's enemies" in place of "David" to avoid putting a curse on him (25:22). If so, the sense is that Yahweh will hold David himself to account if he breaks the covenant.

decisions.choice: saying
decisions.reason: English supplies "saying" to show that the wish is Jonathan's words. Literal brackets it.

source.text: וַיּ֤וֹסֶף יְהֽוֹנָתָן֙ לְהַשְׁבִּ֣יעַ אֶת־דָּוִ֔ד בְּאַהֲבָת֖וֹ אֹת֑וֹ כִּֽי־אַהֲבַ֥ת נַפְשׁ֖וֹ אֲהֵבֽוֹ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And added Jonathan to make swear David by his love [for] him, for [with the] love [of] his soul he loved him.

en.L: And Jonathan again made David swear by his love for him, for he loved him [as] he loved his own soul.
en.B: Jonathan had David swear again by his love for him, because he loved him as he loved himself.
en.R: Jonathan asked David to make his promise once more, because Jonathan loved him. He loved David as much as he loved himself.

decisions.choice: he loved him as his own soul: the love of 18:1-3
decisions.reason: The same words describe how Jonathan first loved David after he killed Goliath (18:1, 3). "His soul" means his own self, his life.

decisions.choice: Jonathan made David swear again
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has Jonathan making David repeat his oath. An ancient Greek translation reads "Jonathan swore again to David". In both, the two friends bind themselves once more.

decisions.choice: by his love for him: the ground of the oath
decisions.reason: The oath rests on Jonathan's love for David. It may be that Jonathan appeals to that love as the reason for the oath, or that David swears by the love between them.

source.text: וַיֹּֽאמֶר־ל֥וֹ יְהוֹנָתָ֖ן מָחָ֣ר חֹ֑דֶשׁ וְנִפְקַ֕דְתָּ כִּ֥י יִפָּקֵ֖ד מוֹשָׁבֶֽךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said to him Jonathan, Tomorrow [is the] new moon, and you will be missed, for will be empty your seat.

en.L: And Jonathan said to him, "Tomorrow [is the] new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty.
en.B: Then Jonathan said to him, "Tomorrow is the new moon festival. You will be missed, because your seat will be empty.
en.R: Then Jonathan said to David, "Tomorrow is the new moon festival. People will notice that you are not there, because your seat will be empty.

decisions.choice: missed ... empty: one verb used twice
decisions.reason: The same verb, which means "to look for and find missing", is used of David being missed and of his seat being empty (verses 6, 25, 27).

decisions.choice: People will notice that you are not there
decisions.reason: Readable names who will miss David and puts the passive verb in active form.

source.text: וְשִׁלַּשְׁתָּ֙ תֵּרֵ֣ד מְאֹ֔ד וּבָאתָ֙ אֶל־הַמָּק֔וֹם אֲשֶׁר־נִסְתַּ֥רְתָּ שָּׁ֖ם בְּי֣וֹם הַֽמַּעֲשֶׂ֑ה וְיָ֣שַׁבְתָּ֔ אֵ֖צֶל הָאֶ֥בֶן הָאָֽזֶל׃

records.literal_gloss: And you will do [it on the] third [day], you will go down greatly, and come to the place where you hid there on [the] day of the deed, and you will stay beside the stone, the Ezel.

en.L: And on the third [day] you will go down quickly and come to the place where you hid yourself on the day of the deed, and stay beside the stone Ezel.
en.B: On the day after tomorrow, go down quickly to the place where you hid when this trouble began, and wait beside the stone Ezel.
en.R: On the day after that, hurry down to the place where you hid before, when all this trouble began. Wait there beside the Ezel stone.

decisions.choice: do it on the third day, go down quickly
decisions.reason: The first verb is formed from the number three and seems to mean "do on the third day" (verses 5 and 12). "Greatly" with "go down" may mean "quickly" or "far down". Both fit a man hurrying to his hiding place.

decisions.choice: the day of the deed: probably when Saul first plotted against David
decisions.reason: This seems to point back to the day when Jonathan told David to hide in the field while he spoke to his father (19:1-3). The phrase is short and its reference is not certain.

decisions.choice: the stone Ezel: a landmark whose name is uncertain
decisions.reason: Ezel appears only here, and the name may mean "departure". An ancient Greek translation reads "beside that mound", and has the same word in verse 41 where the Hebrew has "the south". The place was a landmark in the field near which David could hide.

decisions.choice: when this trouble began; when all this trouble began
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the short phrase "the day of the deed" most likely refers to; see m2.

source.text: וַאֲנִ֕י שְׁלֹ֥שֶׁת הַחִצִּ֖ים צִדָּ֣ה אוֹרֶ֑ה לְשַֽׁלַּֽח־לִ֖י לְמַטָּרָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And I three the arrows to its side will shoot, to send for myself at a target.

en.L: And I will shoot three arrows to its side, as if sending [them] for myself at a target.
en.B: I will shoot three arrows to one side of it, as though I were shooting at a target.
en.R: I will shoot three arrows near the stone, as if I were practicing at a target.

decisions.choice: to its side: beside the stone
decisions.reason: "Its" refers to the stone named in verse 19.

decisions.choice: as if at a target: target practice as a cover
decisions.reason: Jonathan will look as if he is practicing archery, so that no one will suspect a signal. Jonathan was a skilled archer (2 Samuel 1:22).

decisions.choice: practicing at a target
decisions.reason: Readable spells out why shooting at a target would not draw attention.

source.text: וְהִנֵּה֙ אֶשְׁלַ֣ח אֶת־הַנַּ֔עַר לֵ֖ךְ מְצָ֣א אֶת־הַחִצִּ֑ים אִם־אָמֹר֩ אֹמַ֨ר לַנַּ֜עַר הִנֵּ֥ה הַחִצִּ֣ים׀מִמְּךָ֣ וָהֵ֗נָּה קָחֶ֧נּוּ׀וָבֹ֛אָה כִּֽי־שָׁל֥וֹם לְךָ֛ וְאֵ֥ין דָּבָ֖ר חַי־יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And look, I will send the lad, Go, find the arrows. If surely I say to the lad, Look, the arrows [are] from you and hither, take it, and come, for peace [is] to you and there is no thing, [as] lives Yahweh.

en.L: And look, I will send the boy, [saying], 'Go, find the arrows.' If I expressly say to the boy, 'Look, the arrows [are] on this side of you; take them,' then come, for [there is] peace for you and [there is] nothing [wrong], [as] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives.
en.B: Then I will send the boy and tell him, 'Go and find the arrows.' If I say to the boy, 'Look, the arrows are on this side of you; pick them up,' then come, because as surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, you are safe and there is no danger.
en.R: Then I will send my servant boy and tell him, 'Go and find the arrows.' If I shout to him, 'The arrows are on this side of you! Bring them here,' then you can come out. As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, that will mean you are safe. There will be no danger.

decisions.choice: the boy: a young servant
decisions.reason: The word can mean a boy or a young man, and often a servant or attendant (verses 35-40; 14:1). Here he is a young boy who carries Jonathan's weapons and knows nothing of the plan (verse 39).

decisions.choice: come: come out of hiding
decisions.reason: "Come" is the signal for David: he can leave his hiding place and return. The sign means the opposite of the sign in verse 22.

decisions.choice: peace for you and nothing: you are safe and there is no danger
decisions.reason: "Peace" here means safety (verse 7), and "there is no thing" means there is nothing wrong. Jonathan backs the promise with an oath by Yahweh's life (verse 3).

decisions.choice: my servant boy; come out
decisions.reason: Readable says who the boy is and what "come" means for David.

source.text: וְאִם־כֹּ֤ה אֹמַר֙ לָעֶ֔לֶם הִנֵּ֥ה הַחִצִּ֖ים מִמְּךָ֣ וָהָ֑לְאָה לֵ֕ךְ כִּ֥י שִֽׁלַּחֲךָ֖ יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And if thus I say to the young man, Look, the arrows [are] from you and beyond, go, for has sent you away Yahweh.

en.L: But if I say thus to the youth, 'Look, the arrows [are] beyond you,' go, for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has sent you away.
en.B: But if what I tell the young man is, 'Look, the arrows are beyond you,' then go, because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is sending you away.
en.R: But if I shout to the boy, 'The arrows are farther out!' then you must leave. It will mean that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is sending you away.

decisions.choice: youth: another word for the boy
decisions.reason: The word means a young man or lad. It refers to the same servant boy as in verse 21.

decisions.choice: Yahweh has sent you away: David's flight is in God's hands
decisions.reason: Jonathan does not say "my father has driven you away" but "Yahweh has sent you". Even David's escape is seen as part of what Yahweh is doing.

decisions.choice: is sending you away
decisions.reason: The Hebrew past form speaks of what will be settled when the sign is given. Balanced and Readable use the present so that it reads naturally within an instruction about the future.

source.text: וְהַ֨דָּבָ֔ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבַּ֖רְנוּ אֲנִ֣י וָאָ֑תָּה הִנֵּ֧ה יְהוָ֛ה בֵּינִ֥י וּבֵינְךָ֖ עַד־עוֹלָֽם׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And the matter which we have spoken, I and you, look, Yahweh [is] between me and between you forever.

en.L: And [as for] the matter that we have spoken of, I and you, look, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} [is] between me and you forever."
en.B: As for what you and I have agreed, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is witness between you and me forever."
en.R: And remember what we have promised each other. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is the witness between us forever."

decisions.choice: the matter we have spoken: the promises of verses 12-17
decisions.reason: "The matter" is the agreement the two have just made, the covenant and the oaths that bind their families.

decisions.choice: Yahweh between me and you: Yahweh as witness and guard
decisions.reason: To say that Yahweh is "between" two people is to call him to watch over their agreement and to judge whoever breaks it (verse 42; Genesis 31:49-50).

decisions.choice: witness
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "witness" to give the sense of "between"; Literal keeps the bare phrase.

source.text: וַיִּסָּתֵ֥ר דָּוִ֖ד בַּשָּׂדֶ֑ה וַיְהִ֣י הַחֹ֔דֶשׁ וַיֵּ֧שֶׁב הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ אֶל־הַלֶּ֖חֶם לֶאֱכֽוֹל׃

records.literal_gloss: And hid David in the field; and was the new moon, and sat the king at the food to eat.

en.L: So David hid himself in the field. And the new moon came, and the king sat down at the meal to eat.
en.B: So David hid in the field. When the new moon festival came, the king sat down to eat the meal.
en.R: So David hid in the field. When the new moon festival came, the king sat down to eat.

decisions.choice: the food: the festival meal
decisions.reason: The word usually means "bread" but often stands for food or a meal in general (verse 27).

decisions.choice: at the food: the reading noted in the margin
decisions.reason: The consonants in the text read "on" the food, and the scribes' note in the margin reads "to" or "at" it. The sense is the same: the king took his place for the meal.

decisions.choice: new moon festival
decisions.reason: As in verse 5.

source.text: וַיֵּ֣שֶׁב הַ֠מֶּלֶךְ עַל־מ֨וֹשָׁב֜וֹ כְּפַ֣עַם׀בְּפַ֗עַם אֶל־מוֹשַׁב֙ הַקִּ֔יר וַיָּ֨קָם֙ יְה֣וֹנָתָ֔ן וַיֵּ֥שֶׁב אַבְנֵ֖ר מִצַּ֣ד שָׁא֑וּל וַיִּפָּקֵ֖ד מְק֥וֹם דָּוִֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: And sat the king on his seat as time by time, on [the] seat of the wall; and arose Jonathan, and sat Abner from [the] side of Saul; and was empty [the] place of David.

en.L: And the king sat on his seat as [at] other times, on the seat by the wall. And Jonathan rose, and Abner sat by Saul's side, and David's place was empty.
en.B: The king sat in his usual seat by the wall. Jonathan got up, and Abner sat down beside Saul, but David's place was empty.
en.R: The king sat in his usual place by the wall. Jonathan stood up, and Abner sat down next to Saul. But David's seat was empty.

decisions.choice: the seat by the wall: the king's place of honor
decisions.reason: Sitting with his back to the wall, the king faced the room and no one could come at him from behind. The seating at the meal shows each man's rank.

decisions.choice: Jonathan rose
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says that Jonathan "rose", perhaps standing out of respect or giving his seat to Abner. An ancient Greek translation, reading a verb with similar letters, says that Jonathan "was in front", that is, sat facing the king.

decisions.choice: Abner: commander of Saul's army
decisions.reason: Abner son of Ner was Saul's cousin and the commander of his army (14:50-51; 17:55).

decisions.choice: was empty: was missed
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used in verses 6 and 18: David's place was noticed as empty.

source.text: וְלֹֽא־דִבֶּ֥ר שָׁא֛וּל מְא֖וּמָה בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא כִּ֤י אָמַר֙ מִקְרֶ֣ה ה֔וּא בִּלְתִּ֥י טָה֛וֹר ה֖וּא כִּֽי־לֹ֥א טָהֽוֹר׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And not spoke Saul anything on that day, for he said, [An] accident it [is]; not clean he [is], surely not clean.

en.L: But Saul did not say anything on that day, for he said [to himself], "It [is] an accident; he [is] not clean; surely [he is] not clean."
en.B: Saul did not say a word that day. He thought, "Something has happened to him. He is not ritually clean. Surely he is unclean."
en.R: Saul did not say anything about it that day. He thought, "Something must have happened to David to make him unclean. He cannot come to the meal if he is unclean."

decisions.choice: not clean: unfit to share a sacred meal
decisions.reason: The feast included sacrifices, and only people who were ritually clean could eat sacrificial food (Leviticus 7:20-21; 1 Samuel 16:5). Touching a dead body or a bodily discharge could make a man unclean for a day or more (Leviticus 15:16; Numbers 19:11).

decisions.choice: an accident: something that happened by chance
decisions.reason: The word means an event that just happens (6:9). The law uses a related phrase for a man made unclean by what "happens" to him at night (Deuteronomy 23:11).

decisions.choice: surely not clean: Saul convinces himself
decisions.reason: The repeated words show Saul talking himself into an easy explanation, so that he says nothing on the first day.

decisions.choice: said to himself; thought
decisions.reason: Saul "said" these words in his own mind, since he "did not say anything". Literal brackets "to himself"; Balanced and Readable use "thought".

decisions.choice: He cannot come to the meal if he is unclean.
decisions.reason: Readable spells out why being unclean would keep David from the meal; see m1.

source.text: וַיְהִ֗י מִֽמָּחֳרַ֤ת הַחֹ֨דֶשׁ֙ הַשֵּׁנִ֔י וַיִּפָּקֵ֖ד מְק֣וֹם דָּוִ֑דסוַיֹּ֤אמֶר שָׁאוּל֙ אֶל־יְהוֹנָתָ֣ן בְּנ֔וֹ מַדּ֜וּעַ לֹא־בָ֧א בֶן־יִשַׁ֛י גַּם־תְּמ֥וֹל גַּם־הַיּ֖וֹם אֶל־הַלָּֽחֶם׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was on the next day of the new moon, the second, and was empty [the] place of David; and said Saul to Jonathan his son, Why not has come [the] son of Jesse, also yesterday also today, to the meal?

en.L: And it was on the day after the new moon, the second [day], and David's place was empty. And Saul said to Jonathan his son, "Why has the son of Jesse not come to the meal, either yesterday or today?"
en.B: But on the next day, the second day of the new moon festival, David's place was empty again. Saul asked his son Jonathan, "Why has the son of Jesse not come to the meal, either yesterday or today?"
en.R: The next day was the second day of the festival, and David's seat was still empty. So Saul asked his son Jonathan, "Why has Jesse's son not come to eat with us, yesterday or today?"

decisions.choice: the next day of the new moon, the second: the second day of the feast
decisions.reason: The feast lasted two days (verse 34). This is the third day counting from David's talk with Jonathan (verses 5, 12, 19).

decisions.choice: the son of Jesse: a cold way to name David
decisions.reason: Saul does not use David's name. Calling him only "the son of Jesse" makes him a nobody from a common family; Saul does it again (verses 30-31; 22:7-9), and so does Nabal (25:10).

decisions.choice: again; still
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add a word to show that the seat was empty for the second day running.

source.text: וַיַּ֥עַן יְהוֹנָתָ֖ן אֶת־שָׁא֑וּל נִשְׁאֹ֨ל נִשְׁאַ֥ל דָּוִ֛ד מֵעִמָּדִ֖י עַד־בֵּ֥ית לָֽחֶם׃

records.literal_gloss: And answered Jonathan Saul, Asked urgently David from with me [to go] to Bethlehem.

en.L: And Jonathan answered Saul, "David earnestly asked leave of me [to go] to Bethlehem.
en.B: Jonathan answered Saul, "David begged me to let him go to Bethlehem.
en.R: Jonathan answered, "David asked me if he could go to Bethlehem.

decisions.choice: asked urgently: the excuse planned in verse 6
decisions.reason: Jonathan uses the words David gave him (verse 6), with the same doubled verb.

source.text: וַיֹּ֡אמֶר שַׁלְּחֵ֣נִי נָ֡א כִּ֣י זֶבַח֩ מִשְׁפָּחָ֨ה לָ֜נוּ בָּעִ֗יר וְה֤וּא צִוָּֽה־לִי֙ אָחִ֔י וְעַתָּ֗ה אִם־מָצָ֤אתִי חֵן֙ בְּעֵינֶ֔יךָ אִמָּ֥לְטָה נָּ֖א וְאֶרְאֶ֣ה אֶת־אֶחָ֑י עַל־כֵּ֣ן לֹא־בָ֔א אֶל־שֻׁלְחַ֖ן הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And he said, Send me please, for [a] sacrifice of [the] clan [is] for us in the city, and he has commanded me, my brother. And now, if I have found favor in your eyes, let me slip away please and see my brothers. Therefore not he has come to the table of the king.

en.L: He said, 'Please let me go, for our clan has a sacrifice in the city, and my brother has commanded me [to be there]. And now, if I have found favor in your eyes, please let me slip away and see my brothers.' That is why he has not come to the king's table."
en.B: He said, 'Please let me go, because our family is holding a sacrifice in the town, and my brother has told me to be there. So if you are willing, let me get away to see my brothers.' That is why he has not come to the king's table."
en.R: He said, 'Please let me go. Our family is offering a sacrifice in our town, and my brother told me I must be there. If you are my friend, let me slip away to see my brothers.' That is why he has not come to eat at the king's table."

decisions.choice: he has commanded me, my brother: the family's order
decisions.reason: "My brother" is set after the verb for stress. An older brother, perhaps Eliab (16:6; 17:28), seems to be calling the family together, although Jesse was still alive (22:3).

decisions.choice: if I have found favor in your eyes: if you will do me this kindness
decisions.reason: As in verse 3. It is a polite way of asking a favor.

decisions.choice: slip away: get away, escape
decisions.reason: The verb is often used of escaping from danger; it is the verb used of David's escapes from Saul (19:10-12, 17-18). In Jonathan's mouth it sounds like a quick private visit, but the reader hears its other sense.

decisions.choice: if you are willing; if you are my friend
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the polite idiom; Literal keeps "found favor in your eyes".

source.text: וַיִּֽחַר־אַ֤ף שָׁאוּל֙ בִּיה֣וֹנָתָ֔ן וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֔וֹ בֶּֽן־נַעֲוַ֖ת הַמַּרְדּ֑וּת הֲל֣וֹא יָדַ֗עְתִּי כִּֽי־בֹחֵ֤ר אַתָּה֙ לְבֶן־יִשַׁ֔י לְבָ֨שְׁתְּךָ֔ וּלְבֹ֖שֶׁת עֶרְוַ֥ת אִמֶּֽךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And burned [the] anger of Saul against Jonathan, and he said to him, Son of [a] perverse [woman] of rebellion! Do not I know that [you are] choosing the son of Jesse to your shame and to [the] shame of [the] nakedness of your mother?

en.L: And Saul's anger burned against Jonathan, and he said to him, "Son of a perverse, rebellious [woman]! Do I not know that you [are] choosing the son of Jesse, to your own shame and to the shame of your mother's nakedness?
en.B: Saul's anger flared up against Jonathan, and he told him, "You son of a perverse and rebellious woman! Do you think I do not know that you have sided with the son of Jesse? It is a disgrace to you and a disgrace to the mother who bore you.
en.R: Saul became furious with Jonathan. He shouted at him, "You son of a wicked, rebellious woman! I know that you have taken the side of Jesse's son. You are bringing shame on yourself and on your mother who gave birth to you.

decisions.choice: son of a perverse, rebellious woman: an insult aimed at Jonathan
decisions.reason: The insult names Jonathan's mother, but its target is Jonathan: he is called crooked and disloyal, as if by birth. Saul calls his son a traitor.

decisions.choice: choosing: siding with
alternatives: you are a companion of the son of Jesse
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has "choosing", that is, taking David's side. An ancient Greek translation reads "a companion of", from a Hebrew word with similar letters. Either way Saul accuses Jonathan of siding with David against his own father.

decisions.choice: the shame of your mother's nakedness: a disgrace to the mother who bore you
decisions.reason: "Nakedness" here points to the body that gave Jonathan birth. Saul says that Jonathan's choice shames both him and his mother, and so the whole family.

decisions.choice: a disgrace to the mother who bore you
alternatives: to the shame of your mother's nakedness
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the crude expression "your mother's nakedness"; Literal keeps it.

decisions.choice: I know that
decisions.reason: Readable turns Saul's question "Do I not know ...?" into the statement it implies.

source.text: כִּ֣י כָל־הַיָּמִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֤ר בֶּן־יִשַׁי֙ חַ֣י עַל־הָאֲדָמָ֔ה לֹ֥א תִכּ֖וֹן אַתָּ֣ה וּמַלְכוּתֶ֑ךָ וְעַתָּ֗ה שְׁלַ֨ח וְקַ֤ח אֹתוֹ֙ אֵלַ֔י כִּ֥י בֶן־מָ֖וֶת הֽוּא׃ס

records.literal_gloss: For all the days that the son of Jesse lives on the ground, not you will be established, you and your kingdom. And now send and bring him to me, for a son of death he [is].

en.L: For all the days that the son of Jesse lives on the earth, you will not be established, you or your kingdom. And now send and bring him to me, for he [is] a son of death."
en.B: As long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom will be secure. Now send for him and bring him to me, because he must die."
en.R: As long as Jesse's son is alive, neither you nor your kingdom will be safe. Now send someone to bring him to me. He must die!"

decisions.choice: you will not be established: you will not hold the throne
decisions.reason: Saul still thinks of Jonathan as the king to come and of the kingdom as his. Jonathan himself has already given way to David (verses 13-15; 23:17).

decisions.choice: a son of death: someone who must die
decisions.reason: A "son of" something belongs to it. A "son of death" is a man doomed to death or who deserves it (26:16; 2 Samuel 12:5).

decisions.choice: he must die
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the idiom; Literal keeps "son of death".

source.text: וַיַּ֨עַן֙ יְה֣וֹנָתָ֔ן אֶת־שָׁא֖וּל אָבִ֑יו וַיֹּ֧אמֶר אֵלָ֛יו לָ֥מָּה יוּמַ֖ת מֶ֥ה עָשָֽׂה׃

records.literal_gloss: And answered Jonathan Saul his father and said to him, Why should he be put to death? What has he done?

en.L: And Jonathan answered Saul his father and said to him, "Why should he be put to death? What has he done?"
en.B: Jonathan answered his father Saul, "Why should he be put to death? What has he done?"
en.R: Jonathan answered his father, "Why should he die? What has he done wrong?"

decisions.choice: What has he done?: David's own question
decisions.reason: Jonathan asks the question David asked him in verse 1, and pleads as he did before, when Saul listened to him (19:4-6).

source.text: וַיָּ֨טֶל שָׁא֧וּל אֶֽת־הַחֲנִ֛ית עָלָ֖יו לְהַכֹּת֑וֹ וַיֵּ֨דַע֙ יְה֣וֹנָתָ֔ן כִּֽי־כָ֥לָה הִ֛יא מֵעִ֥ם אָבִ֖יו לְהָמִ֥ית אֶת־דָּוִֽד׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And hurled Saul the spear at him to strike him; and knew Jonathan that it had been completed from with his father to put to death David.

en.L: And Saul hurled the spear at him to strike him down. And Jonathan knew that it had been determined by his father to put David to death.
en.B: But Saul threw his spear at him to strike him down. Then Jonathan knew that his father was determined to kill David.
en.R: Then Saul threw his spear at Jonathan to kill him. Now Jonathan knew for sure that his father had decided to kill David.

decisions.choice: Saul hurled the spear: as he had at David
decisions.reason: Saul had twice hurled his spear at David (18:10-11; 19:9-10). Now he turns it on his own son for taking David's side.

decisions.choice: it had been determined: Saul's mind was made up
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used in verses 7 and 9. Saul's anger gives Jonathan the answer he had promised to bring David.

decisions.choice: at Jonathan
decisions.reason: Readable names Jonathan, since "him" could be mistaken for David.

source.text: וַיָּ֧קָם יְהוֹנָתָ֛ן מֵעִ֥ם הַשֻּׁלְחָ֖ן בָּחֳרִי־אָ֑ף וְלֹא־אָכַ֞ל בְּיוֹם־הַחֹ֤דֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִי֙ לֶ֔חֶם כִּ֤י נֶעְצַב֙ אֶל־דָּוִ֔ד כִּ֥י הִכְלִמ֖וֹ אָבִֽיו׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And arose Jonathan from with the table in heat of anger, and not he ate on the day of the new moon, the second, food; for he was grieved for David, for had humiliated him his father.

en.L: And Jonathan rose from the table in hot anger, and he did not eat food on the second day of the new moon, for he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him.
en.B: Jonathan got up from the table in a rage and ate nothing on that second day of the festival. He was grieved for David, since his father had shamed him.
en.R: Jonathan got up from the table very angry. He did not eat anything on that second day of the festival. He was upset about David, because of the shameful way his father had treated him.

decisions.choice: had disgraced him: David, or Jonathan himself
decisions.reason: "Him" most likely means David, whom Saul had insulted and condemned to death (verses 30-31), since Jonathan's grief is "for David". It could also mean Jonathan, whom Saul had shamed before the court (verse 30).

decisions.choice: grieved: deeply pained
decisions.reason: The verb is the one Saul used in his supposed words in verse 3, "or he will be grieved". What Saul wanted to spare Jonathan has now happened.

decisions.choice: because of the shameful way his father had treated him
decisions.reason: Readable keeps "him" open, as the Hebrew does; see m1.

source.text: וַיְהִ֣י בַבֹּ֔קֶר וַיֵּצֵ֧א יְהוֹנָתָ֛ן הַשָּׂדֶ֖ה לְמוֹעֵ֣ד דָּוִ֑ד וְנַ֥עַר קָטֹ֖ן עִמּֽוֹ׃

en.B: Next morning Jonathan went out to the field for the meeting he had arranged with David, and a young boy was with him.
en.R: The next morning Jonathan went out to the field to meet David, as they had agreed. He took a young servant boy with him.

decisions.choice: the appointment: the set time and place
decisions.reason: The word means a fixed time or meeting. It is the meeting agreed in verses 19-22.

decisions.choice: a small boy: a young servant
decisions.reason: As in verse 21. A small boy would not guess that the arrows were a signal.

decisions.choice: servant boy
decisions.reason: Readable says who the boy was; see verse 21.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לְנַעֲר֔וֹ רֻ֗ץ מְצָ֥א נָא֙ אֶת־הַ֣חִצִּ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר אָנֹכִ֖י מוֹרֶ֑ה הַנַּ֣עַר רָ֔ץ וְהֽוּא־יָרָ֥ה הַחֵ֖צִי לְהַעֲבִרֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said to his lad, Run, find please the arrows which I [am] shooting. The lad ran, and he shot the arrow to make it pass beyond him.

en.L: And he said to his boy, "Run, find the arrows that I [am] shooting." The boy ran, and he shot the arrow beyond him.
en.B: He said to his boy, "Run and find the arrows I shoot." As the boy ran, Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him.
en.R: He told the boy, "Run and find the arrows I am going to shoot." While the boy was running, Jonathan shot an arrow past him.

decisions.choice: the arrows ... the arrow: the plan and the first shot
decisions.reason: Jonathan had planned to shoot three arrows (verse 20). The story now follows only the arrow that flew beyond the boy, the one that gives the signal.

decisions.choice: Jonathan
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jonathan as the one who shot, since the last "he" in the sentence is the boy.

source.text: וַיָּבֹ֤א הַנַּ֨עַר֙ עַד־מְק֣וֹם הַחֵ֔צִי אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָרָ֖ה יְהוֹנָתָ֑ן וַיִּקְרָ֨א יְהוֹנָתָ֜ן אַחֲרֵ֤י הַנַּ֨עַר֙ וַיֹּ֔אמֶר הֲל֥וֹא הַחֵ֖צִי מִמְּךָ֥ וָהָֽלְאָה׃

records.literal_gloss: And came the lad to [the] place of the arrow which had shot Jonathan, and called Jonathan after the lad and said, [Is] not the arrow from you and beyond?

en.L: And when the boy came to the place of the arrow that Jonathan had shot, Jonathan called after the boy and said, "[Is] not the arrow beyond you?"
en.B: When the boy came to the spot where Jonathan's arrow had fallen, Jonathan shouted after him, "Is the arrow not beyond you?"
en.R: When the boy came to the spot where the arrow had landed, Jonathan shouted to him, "The arrow is farther out!"

decisions.choice: beyond you: the signal of danger
decisions.reason: These are the words agreed in verse 22. They tell David that Saul means to kill him and that he must go.

decisions.choice: The arrow is farther out!
decisions.reason: Readable gives Jonathan's question as the statement it implies, in the words of verse 22.

source.text: וַיִּקְרָ֤א יְהֽוֹנָתָן֙ אַחֲרֵ֣י הַנַּ֔עַר מְהֵרָ֥ה ח֖וּשָׁה אַֽל־תַּעֲמֹ֑ד וַיְלַקֵּ֞ט נַ֤עַר יְהֽוֹנָתָן֙ אֶת־הַ֣חִצִּ֔ים וַיָּבֹ֖א אֶל־אֲדֹנָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And called Jonathan after the lad, Quickly! Hurry! Do not stand! And gathered [the] lad of Jonathan the arrows and came to his master.

en.L: And Jonathan called after the boy, "Quickly! Hurry! Do not stand [still]!" And Jonathan's boy gathered the arrows and came to his master.
en.B: Then Jonathan shouted after the boy, "Hurry! Be quick! Do not stop!" Jonathan's boy picked up the arrows and came back to his master.
en.R: Then he shouted, "Hurry! Go fast! Do not stop!" The boy picked up the arrows and brought them back to his master.

decisions.choice: Quickly! Hurry! Do not stand still!: words for two hearers
decisions.reason: Jonathan shouts to the boy, but the words also tell David, hidden nearby, to flee without delay.

decisions.choice: the arrows: the reading noted in the margin
decisions.reason: The consonants in the text read "the arrow", and the scribes' note in the margin reads "the arrows". The boy picked up whatever arrows had been shot.

source.text: וְהַנַּ֖עַר לֹֽא־יָדַ֣ע מְא֑וּמָה אַ֤ךְ יְהֽוֹנָתָן֙ וְדָוִ֔ד יָדְע֖וּ אֶת־הַדָּבָֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And the lad not knew anything; only Jonathan and David knew the matter.

en.L: And the boy did not know anything; only Jonathan and David knew the matter.
en.B: The boy knew nothing of what it meant; only Jonathan and David knew.
en.R: The boy did not understand what was going on. Only Jonathan and David knew what it meant.

decisions.choice: the matter: the meaning of the sign
decisions.reason: "The matter" is the plan and its message (verse 23). The boy saw only target practice.

decisions.choice: what it meant
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the boy did not know.

source.text: וַיִּתֵּ֤ן יְהֽוֹנָתָן֙ אֶת־כֵּלָ֔יו אֶל־הַנַּ֖עַר אֲשֶׁר־ל֑וֹ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֔וֹ לֵ֖ךְ הָבֵ֥יא הָעִֽיר׃

records.literal_gloss: And gave Jonathan his weapons to the lad who [was] with him, and said to him, Go, bring [them to] the city.

en.L: And Jonathan gave his weapons to the boy who [was] with him, and said to him, "Go, take [them to] the city."
en.B: Then Jonathan gave his weapons to the boy and told him, "Go, carry them back to town."
en.R: Then Jonathan gave his bow and arrows to the boy and said, "Take these back to town."

decisions.choice: his weapons: his bow and arrows
decisions.reason: The word covers any gear or equipment; here it is Jonathan's archery equipment.

decisions.choice: go to the city: Jonathan sends the boy away
decisions.reason: With the boy gone, Jonathan and David can meet without a witness for a last farewell.

decisions.choice: bow and arrows
decisions.reason: Readable names the weapons, since only Jonathan's archery gear is in view.

source.text: הַנַּעַר֮ בָּא֒ וְדָוִ֗ד קָ֚ם מֵאֵ֣צֶל הַנֶּ֔גֶב וַיִּפֹּ֨ל לְאַפָּ֥יו אַ֛רְצָה וַיִּשְׁתַּ֖חוּ שָׁלֹ֣שׁ פְּעָמִ֑ים וַֽיִּשְּׁק֣וּ׀אִ֣ישׁ אֶת־רֵעֵ֗הוּ וַיִּבְכּוּ֙ אִ֣ישׁ אֶת־רֵעֵ֔הוּ עַד־דָּוִ֖ד הִגְדִּֽיל׃

records.literal_gloss: The lad went, and David arose from beside the south, and fell on his face to the ground and bowed three times; and they kissed each his friend, and wept each with his friend, until David did great.

en.L: The boy went, and David rose from beside the south [side], and he fell on his face to the ground and bowed down three times. And they kissed each other and wept with each other, until David [wept] the more.
en.B: As soon as the boy had gone, David got up from his place by the south side and fell with his face to the ground, bowing down three times. Then they kissed each other and wept together, and David wept the more.
en.R: As soon as the boy was gone, David came out from his hiding place on the south side. He bowed down three times with his face to the ground. Then they kissed each other and cried together. David cried even harder than Jonathan.

decisions.choice: from beside the south: from his hiding place
decisions.reason: The Hebrew reads "from beside the south", probably the south side of the stone or field. An ancient Greek translation reads "from beside the mound", the same word it has in place of "Ezel" in verse 19.

decisions.choice: bowed three times: deep respect
decisions.reason: Falling to the ground and bowing showed honor to someone of higher rank. David honors Jonathan as the king's son and as the one who has saved his life.

decisions.choice: they kissed each other: a farewell between friends
decisions.reason: Kissing was a usual greeting and farewell among relatives and close friends (Genesis 29:13; 31:28; Ruth 1:9, 14).

decisions.choice: until David did great: David wept the more
decisions.reason: The words are short and unusual. They most likely mean that David's weeping grew greater than Jonathan's. Some read them as "until David recovered himself".

decisions.choice: his place by the south side; his hiding place on the south side
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say where David had been, from verses 19-22.

records.literal_gloss: And said Jonathan to David, Go in peace, because we have sworn, the two of us, we, in [the] name of Yahweh, saying, Yahweh will be between me and between you, and between my offspring and between your offspring, forever.

en.L: And Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace, since we have sworn, the two of us, in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, saying, '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever.'"
en.B: Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace. We two have sworn in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, saying, '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will be witness between me and you, and between my descendants and your descendants, forever.'"
en.R: Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace. We have both made a promise in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. We said, '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will be the witness between you and me, and between your descendants and my descendants, forever.'"

decisions.choice: verse numbers: the Hebrew text ends chapter 20 here
decisions.reason: This translation numbers verses as the Hebrew text does. In the Hebrew text chapter 20 ends with Jonathan's words, and the next sentence, "And he rose and went, and Jonathan went into the city", is 21:1. Many Bibles print that sentence as the second half of 20:42 and so number the rest of chapter 21 one lower (Hebrew 21:2-16 is 21:1-15 there). The words are the same; only the numbers differ.

decisions.choice: Yahweh will be between me and you: Yahweh as witness
decisions.reason: As in verse 23: Yahweh watches over the oath and will judge whoever breaks it.

decisions.choice: my offspring and your offspring forever: an oath for the generations
decisions.reason: The oath binds the descendants of both men. David kept it when he was king (2 Samuel 9:1-7; 21:7).

decisions.choice: go in peace: go safely, with my blessing
decisions.reason: A farewell that wishes the other well (1:17; 25:35). Here it comes with the reason David can go in peace: the oath that still binds them.

decisions.choice: witness
decisions.reason: As in verse 23, Balanced and Readable add "witness" to give the sense of "between".
